explanation:
Work through the question before opening the mark scheme.

Key ideas:
• Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
• For the diver's motion in air, either use conservation of energy or resolve the initial velocity and use constant-acceleration equations.
• In water, identify every vertical force and choose a sign convention before applying F = ma.
• Drag depends on speed: as the diver slows, the drag force decreases.
• For the final acceleration, calculate the resultant force first, then divide by mass. State the direction as well as the magnitude.

Use the Official Mark Scheme tab to see exactly which intermediate steps and statements Cambridge awards marks for.

This question links stress, strain, Young modulus and elastic energy.

Useful route:
1. Read the stress corresponding to the stated strain from the graph.
2. Use stress = force / cross-sectional area, with A = πd²/4.
3. Young modulus is stress / strain in the linear elastic region.
4. For elastic energy, use the area under the force-extension graph (or 1/2 Fx when appropriate).

Be especially careful to convert mm to m and GPa to Pa. Compare your numerical working with the Official Mark Scheme to see where Cambridge places C/A marks.

Treat upward as positive and keep the sign convention consistent.

The ball initially moves upward, slows under the constant downward acceleration g, reaches v = 0 at its highest point, then accelerates downward. Constant-acceleration equations connect displacement, velocity and time.

For the graph part, use the physics rather than drawing by appearance: with negligible air resistance the acceleration is constant, so a velocity-time graph must have constant gradient.

Start by defining the system and a positive direction.

For the collision:
• total momentum before = total momentum after;
• include velocity signs, not just speeds;
• solve for the unknown velocity.

To decide whether a collision is perfectly elastic, compare total kinetic energy before and after. Momentum conservation alone does NOT establish that a collision is elastic.

The Official Mark Scheme shows the exact statements/calculations needed for each mark.

Choose the boat+sack as the system during the short collision.

1. State conservation of momentum correctly: total momentum of an isolated system remains constant.
2. Write momentum before = momentum after, including both masses in the final combined mass because the sack remains attached.
3. For the energy comparison, calculate total kinetic energy before and after separately.
4. If kinetic energy decreases, the collision is inelastic even though momentum is conserved.

Keep momentum (kg m s⁻¹) distinct from kinetic energy (J).

Use the wave definitions precisely.

Period is the time for one complete oscillation at a point. Frequency and period satisfy f = 1/T. Wave speed, frequency and wavelength satisfy v = fλ.

For diffraction/interference parts, identify the relevant path/wavelength condition before substituting numbers. Keep angles and orders clearly labelled, and use SI units for wavelength when calculating.

topic: Potential difference; electrical energy; circuit quantities
Potential difference; charge carriers; drift speed
Charge; current; number density; drift speed
Definition of current; terminal p.d.; electrical power
First law; series power; LDR potential divider
explanation: Start with Kirchhoff's first law: current entering a junction equals current leaving it. For the two series resistors, the current is the same, so compare powers using P=I^2 R. For the LDR circuit use I=5.4/1800=0.0030 A. The LDR has 9.0-5.4=3.6 V across it, giving R_L=3.6/0.0030=1200 ohm. As illumination increases, R_L falls, total resistance falls, current rises and the voltage across the fixed resistor increases.

solution_steps.title: Kirchhoff's first law
solution_steps.body: At any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum leaving: \(\sum I_{\mathrm{in}}=\sum I_{\mathrm{out}}\). This expresses conservation of charge.

solution_steps.title: The two resistors X and Y are in parallel
solution_steps.body: Parallel components have the same potential difference. Hence \(P=V^2/R\); since \(R_X>R_Y\), resistor **Y** dissipates more power. From \(R=\rho L/A\) (same material and length), **Y** also has the larger cross-sectional area.

solution_steps.title: Current and LDR resistance
solution_steps.body: \(I=5.4/1800=3.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm A\). Across the LDR, \(V_L=9.0-5.4=3.6\,\mathrm V\); therefore \(R_L=3.6/(3.0\times10^{-3})=\boxed{1200\,\Omega}\).

solution_steps.title: Effect of brighter light
solution_steps.body: The resistance of the LDR decreases. Series resistance decreases, so the circuit current rises. The p.d. across the fixed resistor \(V=I\times1800\) consequently increases.

topic: Kirchhoff voltage law; switching a resistor network
explanation: Apply Kirchhoff's second law to a closed loop: sum of electromotive forces equals sum of potential differences. Identify which resistors share current (series) and which share a potential difference (parallel). Compare the switch-open and switch-closed circuits by redrawing each configuration before applying V=IR.

solution_steps.title: Loop law
solution_steps.body: Write \(\sum\mathcal E=\sum IR\) around a closed loop; the signs must follow your chosen direction.

solution_steps.title: Switch-open case
solution_steps.body: Trace the actual conducting branches in Fig. 6.1 and redraw the active network. Decide which resistors have common current and which have common p.d. before applying \(V=IR\).

solution_steps.title: Switch-closed case
solution_steps.body: Repeat with the switch closed, checking whether a branch is bypassed. Apply both \(I_\mathrm{in}=I_\mathrm{out}\) and the loop rule if the circuit has a junction.

solution_steps.title: Self-check
solution_steps.body: Compare both arrangements against the Cambridge mark scheme; explain the physical reason for any changed currents or p.d.s.

topic: Kirchhoff current law; series resistance and internal resistance
explanation: Kirchhoff's first law expresses conservation of charge. For two series resistors the loop law gives V=V_1+V_2=I(R_1+R_2), so R_T=R_1+R_2. Here I=1.35/(10+15)=0.054 A and the lost volts are 1.50-1.35=0.15 V. Therefore r=0.15/0.054≈2.8 ohm. When R_3 is added in the configuration shown, reconsider the external equivalent resistance before judging the cell current and terminal p.d.

solution_steps.title: First law
solution_steps.body: \(\sum I_{\mathrm{in}}=\sum I_{\mathrm{out}}\). No charge accumulates at a junction in the steady state.

solution_steps.title: Derive the series rule
solution_steps.body: Using the loop law, \(V=V_1+V_2\). Since the current \(I\) is the same in each series resistor, \(IR_T=IR_1+IR_2\), hence \(\boxed{R_T=R_1+R_2}\).

solution_steps.title: Calculate internal resistance
solution_steps.body: \(I=1.35/(10+15)=0.054\,\mathrm A\). Lost volts: \(E-V=1.50-1.35=0.15\,\mathrm V\). Hence \(r=(E-V)/I=0.15/0.054=\boxed{2.8\,\Omega}\) to two significant figures.

solution_steps.title: Adding the extra resistor
solution_steps.body: The external equivalent resistance decreases, so current from the cell **increases**. Because the cell has internal resistance, \(Ir\) increases and the terminal p.d. \(V=E-Ir\) **decreases**.

topic: Kirchhoff second law; variable resistor and thermistor
explanation: Use the second law around the series loop: E=V_X+V_Y. For part (b)(i), V_X=9.0-4.0=5.0 V. Hence R_X=5.0/(1.1×10^-2)≈455 ohm. To find the new p.d. of Y, read its resistance at 190 Celsius from the graph, calculate I=9.0/(R_X+R_Y), then V_Y=IR_Y. Increasing R_X reduces the series current, so V_Y decreases when R_Y remains fixed.

solution_steps.title: Kirchhoff's second law
solution_steps.body: For any closed loop, the algebraic sum of electromotive forces equals the sum of potential differences. Equivalently, \(\sum\Delta V=0\).

solution_steps.title: Calculate the resistance of X
solution_steps.body: The components are in series: \(V_X=9.0-4.0=5.0\,\mathrm V\). Thus \(R_X=V_X/I=5.0/(1.1\times10^{-2})\approx\boxed{450\,\Omega}\), consistent with the official rounded result.

solution_steps.title: Read the graph and find the new p.d.
solution_steps.body: At \(190\,^\circ\mathrm C\), read \(R_Y\approx25\,\Omega\). Use the potential-divider relationship \(V_Y=E\,R_Y/(R_X+R_Y)=9.0(25)/(450+25)=\boxed{0.47\,\mathrm V}\).

solution_steps.title: Explain the final change
solution_steps.body: Increasing \(R_X\) increases total series resistance, so current falls. Since \(R_Y\) is constant at that temperature, \(V_Y=IR_Y\) **decreases**.

topic: Kirchhoff laws; parallel resistance and cell internal resistance
explanation: The second law is conservation of energy around a loop. For the parallel resistors, first law gives I=I_1+I_2 and both branches have the same p.d., V. Using I=V/R_T, I_1=V/R_1 and I_2=V/R_2 yields 1/R_T=1/R_1+1/R_2. For the numerical parts use E=I(R_T+r) and terminal p.d. V=E-Ir. Adding a parallel resistor reduces R_T, increases the cell current, and (for nonzero r) decreases terminal p.d.

solution_steps.title: State the second law
solution_steps.body: The sum of electromotive forces around a closed loop equals the sum of potential differences; it follows from conservation of energy.

solution_steps.title: Parallel combination proof
solution_steps.body: At the junction, \(I=I_1+I_2\) (first law). The p.d. is common to each parallel branch: \(V=IR_T=I_1R_1=I_2R_2\). Substituting currents gives \(\boxed{1/R_T=1/R_1+1/R_2}\).

solution_steps.title: Cell with internal resistance
solution_steps.body: Calculate \(R_T\) for the external parallel combination. Then use \(E=I(R_T+r)\) and \(V=E-Ir\) as required.

solution_steps.title: Adding a further parallel branch
solution_steps.body: Equivalent external resistance decreases; the current through the cell increases. Because the cell loses more volts internally (\(Ir\)), its terminal p.d. **decreases**.

topic: Kirchhoff second law; cells in parallel and resistance
explanation: For three identical cells in parallel, the equivalent electromotive force remains 1.5 V while the effective internal resistance is 0.590/3≈0.197 ohm. Since the total circuit resistance is 2.2 ohm, external resistance is ≈2.0 ohm. Current is I=1.5/2.2≈0.682 A. For cylindrical sections of equal length and material, R=ρL/A so the resistance ratio is the inverse area ratio. For drift speed, I=nAvq; identical current means drift speed is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area.

solution_steps.title: Second law
solution_steps.body: The sum of electromotive forces equals the sum of potential differences around a closed loop.

solution_steps.title: Cells in parallel
solution_steps.body: For three identical cells in parallel, their net e.m.f. remains \(1.5\,\mathrm V\) and internal resistances are in parallel: \(r_\mathrm{eq}=0.590/3=0.197\,\Omega\).

solution_steps.title: External conductor resistance and current
solution_steps.body: Total resistance \(2.2\,\Omega\) includes internal resistance. Thus \(R_\mathrm{conductor}=2.2-0.197\approx\boxed{2.0\,\Omega}\). Then \(I=E/R_\mathrm{total}=1.5/2.2\approx\boxed{0.68\,\mathrm A}\).

solution_steps.title: Geometric ratios
solution_steps.body: For the same material and length, \(R\propto1/A\propto1/d^2\), so \(R_A/R_B=(d_B/d_A)^2=(7.6/4.3)^2\approx3.1\). Since current in A and B is equal, \(v\propto1/A\), giving the same ratio for \(v_A/v_B\).

topic: Kirchhoff first law; thermistor and internal resistance
explanation: At a junction, incoming current equals outgoing current. A negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor has falling resistance as temperature increases. Analyse which branches are in parallel and which elements are in series, then use the first law for the current split. For the cell, terminal p.d. is V=E-Ir. If the cell current grows, the lost volts Ir grow and the terminal p.d. falls.

solution_steps.title: The first law
solution_steps.body: At a junction, total incoming current equals total outgoing current.

solution_steps.title: Negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor
solution_steps.body: As temperature rises, its resistance falls; sketch a decreasing, curved resistance–temperature graph starting at \(R_0\).

solution_steps.title: Analyse the circuit
solution_steps.body: Redraw the current paths and identify series and parallel parts before calculating. Apply \(I_\mathrm{in}=\sum I_\mathrm{out}\) at junctions and \(V=IR\) in each branch.

solution_steps.title: Include internal resistance
solution_steps.body: Terminal potential difference is \(V=E-Ir\). Evaluate how the cell current changes when thermistor resistance drops, then how \(Ir\) and \(V\) change.

topic: Kirchhoff first law; LDR branches and terminal potential difference
explanation: Kirchhoff first law: total battery current equals the sum of branch currents. The terminal p.d. is V=E-Ir=5.0-(0.038)(4.7)=4.82 V, hence about 4.8 V. Use the resistor X current I_1=V/100, then Kirchhoff's law to determine I_2 with the actual branch arrangement shown in Fig. 5.1. For the power of Y, use P=I_2²R_Y. Decreasing incident light increases the LDR resistance, changing the total current and therefore the lost volts Ir.

solution_steps.title: First law
solution_steps.body: At a junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum of currents leaving: \(\sum I_\mathrm{in}=\sum I_\mathrm{out}\).

solution_steps.title: Terminal p.d. of the battery
solution_steps.body: \(V=E-Ir=5.0-(38\times10^{-3})(4.7)=4.8214\,\mathrm V\approx\boxed{4.8\,\mathrm V}\).

solution_steps.title: Split of current between branches
solution_steps.body: Read \(R_Z=120\,\Omega\) from the graph. The branch containing X and Z has current \(I_1=4.8/(100+120)\approx0.022\,\mathrm A\). From Kirchhoff's first law, \(I_2=0.038-I_1\approx\boxed{0.016\,\mathrm A}\).

solution_steps.title: Power in resistor Y
solution_steps.body: \(P_Y=I_2V\approx0.016\times4.8=\boxed{0.077\,\mathrm W}\).

solution_steps.title: Reducing illumination
solution_steps.body: The LDR resistance rises; battery current falls. Thus the internal voltage loss \(Ir\) falls and terminal p.d. \(V=E-Ir\) **increases**.

topic: Kirchhoff loop rule; series and parallel resistors with internal resistance
explanation: Use Kirchhoff's second law: E=I(R_ext+r) for the cell. In series, R_ext=R_1+R_2; in parallel, 1/R_ext=1/R_1+1/R_2. In each circuit compute the new total resistance before calculating current. Remember that adding a parallel path decreases equivalent external resistance, but a real cell also has internal resistance.

solution_steps.title: Series circuit
solution_steps.body: Use the loop rule \(E=I(R_1+R_2+r)\). The cell's internal resistance \(r\) must be included in the total.

solution_steps.title: Parallel circuit
solution_steps.body: Once the two external resistors are reconnected in parallel, use \(R_\mathrm{ext}=R_1R_2/(R_1+R_2)\), followed by \(I=E/(R_\mathrm{ext}+r)\).

solution_steps.title: Compare cell currents
solution_steps.body: The external equivalent resistance decreases in the parallel arrangement, so cell current rises. Follow the original circuit diagram carefully when describing the new branch currents.

mcq_explanation: Kirchhoff's first law concerns current at a junction: the algebraic sum of currents is zero because electric charge is conserved. The second law concerns energy around a complete loop. Hence A.
The first law follows from conservation of charge at a junction. The second law follows from conservation of energy around a loop. The correct pairing is charge / energy, so A.

The first law is charge conservation: total current entering a junction equals total current leaving it. The second law is energy conservation: the algebraic sum of potential changes in a closed loop is zero. Therefore A.
Use Kirchhoff's first law at the junction. The directions of the arrows give a resultant current in wire R of 2 A. Then use \(Q=I\Delta t\): \(Q=2\times5=\boxed{10\ \mathrm C}\). Hence C.

Kirchhoff's first law states that current entering a junction equals current leaving it. Current is the flow of charge per second, so the underlying conserved quantity is charge, not energy or momentum. Therefore A.
